title: Commercial farming

blocks.heading: Commercial farming
blocks.text: Commercial farming produces primarily for sale and can use varied scales, technologies and crop arrangements. It differs from subsistence farming primarily meeting household needs. Market orientation does not by itself establish large scale, monoculture or sustainable practice.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Farming tools and technology
blocks.text: Equipment can assist planting, irrigation, harvesting or processing. It can improve timeliness or capacity if suitable inputs, operators and repair support exist; an expensive unused machine does not raise useful production.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Monoculture and scale
blocks.text: Monoculture is growing a single crop over an area, often repeatedly; distinguish it from rotating different crops. Specialisation can simplify equipment and marketing but can concentrate pest, weather and price risks. Large scale and monoculture are separate features.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Plantations
blocks.text: A plantation is an estate producing a commercial crop, often a perennial crop, organised for market supply. Concentrated output can support processing and employment, but land access, labour conditions and dependence on one market affect the development result.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Crop rotation
blocks.text: Crop rotation is growing different crops in a planned sequence on the same land over time. A suitable sequence can help manage soil conditions and interrupt some pest cycles. It differs from repeating one crop or mixing several crops at the same time.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Read farm organisation
blocks.text: Describe this fictional comparison: Farm A repeats one crop and receives all crop revenue from it; B rotates crops and earns revenue from three. A concentrates crop and income exposure; B combines crop rotation with a more varied revenue base. A price fall in one crop therefore exposes a larger share of A’s recorded crop income.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Connect this lesson to Production (3.1), Sustainable Development (1.2) and Urbanisation (4.2). Identify the livelihood or resource constraint, trace the mechanism and distinguish a feasible action from a hoped-for outcome. The cases here are fictional, not claims about a named present-day community.
